source.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
source.authors: Maximilian Dreyer; Erblina Purelku; Johanna Vielhaben; W. Samek; S. Lapuschkin

record.tranche_reason: The study measures polysemanticity in pretrained image classifiers using feature visualizations and CLIP embedding distances, rather than reproducing the original circuit-analysis method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own polysemanticity measurements and purification outcomes. It also cites prior work on polysemanticity, which is not recorded as a result. It uses the top 100 activating samples and compares clustering choices; values displayed only in plots are not transcribed as numbers.
record.test_reason: Measures how polysemantic neurons are in ImageNet ResNets. It clusters CLIP embeddings of cropped top-activating samples, reporting a distribution over all penultimate neurons and named examples. This is a different method from Zoom In's feature visualization and circuits, aimed at the same question (V1). The appendix also shows that CLIP and attribution scoring disagree on whether some neurons are mixed (V7, and partly V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that polysemantic ResNet neurons can be split into purer virtual neurons by clustering lower-layer circuit attributions. PURE beats activation-based clustering by CLIP scores and comes close to DINOv2. They also note that most penultimate neurons appear rather monosemantic, with a few hundred of 2048 ResNet-50 neurons clearly polysemantic. CLIP is an imperfect judge of semantic disentanglement.
record.recipe_differences: PURE uses a partial backward pass with Gradient×Activation attributions, clusters the attributions of the 100 most activating samples, and evaluates cropped feature visualizations with CLIP and DINOv2. It is not a reproduction of the original circuit method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported separation depends on clustering method (PURE versus activations), number of clusters, architecture, and evaluation embedding/criterion. The paper notes disagreement between CLIP and attribution-based clusterings and ambiguity between visual and semantic separation.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower-layer Gradient×Activation attributions for a neuron's top samples form distinct clusters, which the authors read as separate circuits per feature. Splitting by these clusters separates features better than splitting by activations, by CLIP distance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The distinct features of a polysemantic neuron are computed through distinguishable upstream circuits, so the neuron can be split post hoc into monosemantic virtual neurons.

record.problems: The paper treats CLIP and DINOv2 as indicators of interpretability but says human feedback or controlled evaluation would be valuable. It does not report a large ablation study, does not compare architectures conclusively, and does not measure task-performance costs. Several plotted distributions and comparisons have no numerical values stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The additional qualitative neurons in Appendix A.3 and figures A.4-A.6 are not all separately rowed; rows include examples with explicit text descriptions or particularly clear stated outcomes. The detailed activation-clustering divergences in Appendix A.4.1, Fig. A.9, are not separately rowed because they do not add a distinct conclusion beyond the reported method- and evaluator-dependence.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 and its specific examples (e.g. neuron 4e:55, cat faces/cars); layers other than the penultimate layer.
Not tested. The authors hypothesise shared circuit nodes, not superposition, and do not test capacity.
Activation function and regularization are not varied, and there is no performance cost. The ResNet depth comparison is hedged and deferred to future work.
Whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare across neurons; canonical InceptionV1 neurons.
Which part of the activation range is examined (only the top 100 samples are used).

missing.what: Statement on prevalence: inter-cluster distance falls as k rises, which the authors read as 'most neurons are rather monosemantic'. For ResNet-50 they say only a few hundred of 2048 are more polysemantic.
Fig. 1 example neuron mixing 'hairy dog' and 'maze', split by PURE into two virtual neurons.

Named monosemantic examples from randomly sampled neurons (#162, #1804) and from low-separability neurons (#1 'chain', #160 'seashore'). These give context on the share of neurons that are polysemantic.

record.verdict_notes: The study's method-vs-baseline rows (r19-r22) are moved to 'none'. No V5 verdict is given: the only architecture comparison is hedged, deferred by the authors, and confounded by differing neuron counts. The paper's mechanism hypothesis (shared circuit nodes) is stated but not tested against superposition. Neuron #1028 carries two different labels in the paper. V1 support comes from a non-original setting (ResNets), so it is not self-confirmation.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55 or the specific cat-face/car-front/cat-leg examples.
No transformer language models or language-model neurons.
Does not test whether superposition or feature-to-neuron capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes when capacity is sufficient.
Compares ResNet architectures only; does not vary activation functions or regularization, and does not measure task-performance cost from lowering polysemanticity.
Does not establish that canonical unrelated mixtures are actually one shared feature or that such mixtures are rare.
Does not systematically vary the activation range examined; uses the 100 most activating samples. It compares clustering/attribution measures and discusses limitations of CLIP-based scoring.

rows.subject: ResNet-101
rows.operation_detail: Compares CLIP cluster-separation scores for PURE attribution clustering, activation clustering, and DINOv2-embedding clustering.
rows.measure: CLIP inter- and intra-cluster embedding distances
rows.baseline: Activation-based clustering; DINOv2 clustering is also shown as a baseline
rows.value: PURE produces more disentangled representations than activation-based clustering and is described as performance-wise close to DINOv2 clustering.
rows.note: This compares methods for identifying separable feature visualizations; no classifier performance cost is measured.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (PURE) with activation and DINOv2 clustering. This is purification performance, not polysemanticity or measurement dependence of the label.

rows.subject: ResNet-34 and ResNet-50
rows.size_stated: ResNet-34 penultimate layer has 512 neurons; ResNet-50 has 2048 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Compares CLIP cluster-separation results for PURE and activation-based clustering across cluster counts.
rows.value: The paper states that PURE gives better cluster separation than activation-based clustering for all experiments. As cluster count rises, intra-cluster distances generally fall, while inter-cluster distance often falls.
rows.note: The authors note that falling inter-cluster distance as cluster count increases suggests most neurons are rather monosemantic.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method with a baseline across k. The aside that most neurons are rather monosemantic belongs in a separate prevalence row (see missing).

rows.subject: ResNet-50 neurons #614 and #1055
rows.operation_detail: Compares PURE-attribution clustering with CLIP-embedding clustering of reference samples.
rows.value: The paper reports divergence for both neurons; small attribution distances among same-class samples lead to clustering that is not aligned with CLIP.
rows.note: The paper states that CLIP can separate object classes even where the model's semantics may be shared, so visual and semantic separation need not coincide.
rows.check: Whether a neuron's samples split into distinct groups differs between attribution-based and CLIP-based scoring. This is the V7 effect in full, so the state should be observed, not partial.

source_check.correct: For #614 and #1055, PURE attributions 'can result in different clustering (compared to CLIP)'. Very small distances between same-class samples (lacewing, buckeye) give 'unaligned clustering'. Both methods split into k=2 clusters, and the text does not say either judges the neuron mixed or pure. V7 state: partial.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 neuron #271
rows.operation_detail: Compares PURE-attribution clustering with CLIP-embedding clustering of reference samples.
rows.measure: Agreement between visual clustering and inferred semantics
rows.value: The paper describes a shared triangular-shape semantics in toy windmills and dog ears, while CLIP separates dogs from windmills.
rows.note: The authors cite this as a limitation of using CLIP as an evaluator of semantic disentanglement.
rows.check: CLIP splits dogs from windmills, while attributions show one shared 'triangular shape' semantic. So the polysemantic verdict depends on the scorer (V7 observed), and an apparent mixture is one shared feature (V6 observed for this neuron).
